name: Uma Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I translate Spanish into English, mostly medical stuff: patient leaflets, consent forms for drug trials, the odd hospital discharge letter. Nearly all of it comes through one agency in the city that works for drug companies. I work from my bedroom in a flat I share with my friend Noor, and I'm usually at the desk by eight with headphones on. On Thursday evenings I volunteer at the migrant legal clinic on Albion Road, interpreting for people filling in asylum and housing forms.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best and worst of it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The best is when a consent form finally reads like something a scared patient could understand. The worst is the money. The agency pays me less than they paid the person before me, I've got a student loan, and I've never had more than about three weeks of rent saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good news for patients, honestly, because medical translation needs someone who knows that 'may cause drowsiness' isn't the same as 'can make you sleepy' in a legal sense. At the clinic I'd tell the volunteers we're not about to be replaced. Online I'd stay out of it, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved but not secure. My agency already runs everything through a machine first and asks me to check it, and they pay less for that. That stays the same in this picture, so I'm still one rate cut away from not making rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with the agency and try to get one more direct client, maybe the university hospital's research office, so I'm not relying on one source. I'd try putting aside forty a month, which I keep saying and never quite do. I'd keep the clinic Thursdays, because that's the bit of the week I actually like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly flat. It's not fear, it's that same tiredness of always being just about OK.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use the machine first sometimes. How do you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use it when the agency sends a sixty-page trial protocol with a three-day deadline, because otherwise I can't physically do it. Then I check every line. Half the time the machine translation is fine, and half the time it's quietly wrong in a way that could hurt someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about getting that direct client?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dr Ruiz at the research office, who I met through the clinic. She once said they struggle to find Spanish translators who understand trial paperwork. I've been meaning to email her for about six months.

say: **Medical translation** still needs a person who knows what the words mean legally.
Volunteers at the clinic **aren't being replaced** anytime soon.
think: I'm **one rate cut** away from not making rent, AI or not.
My agency already **pays less** for checking machine drafts.
do: Email the hospital **research office** about direct work this winter.
Put aside **forty a month** from now on.
feel: **Tired** of always being just about OK, rather than afraid.
S0.quote: Half the time the machine translation is fine, and half the time it's quietly wrong in a way that could hurt someone.
fieldNote: Her stress is **money already**, not AI: one agency, a loan and three weeks saved.
She uses machine drafts **only under pressure**, then checks every line.
The clinic is where her **values** live; the agency is where her rent comes from.

steps.text: Email Dr Ruiz at the research office about direct translation work
Set up an automatic transfer of forty a month into savings
Keep interpreting at the Albion Road clinic on Thursdays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the drug companies are saving millions and the translators are paying for it. I'd share the research on medical errors in machine translation, and I'd want rules saying a qualified human has to sign off any patient document. That's not anti-technology, it's basic safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my agency would halve the number of translators it uses within a couple of years. I'm average, not the best, so I might not be one of the ones they keep. The checking work would keep coming, but at a rate I couldn't live on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join or help start a translators' co-op, so we could sell directly to hospitals and charities instead of through agencies. I'd do a proper course in using the tools well, since by then other people would have shown which ones actually work. And I'd ask Noor if we could move somewhere cheaper next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry and a bit frightened. I'd also feel slightly guilty, because I'd be using the same tools that are cutting my rates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might not be one they keep. What makes you think that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a woman at the agency, Inés, who has twenty years in pharma and knows every regulator by name. If they keep five people, she's first. I'm the one they ring when everyone else is busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a contradiction in fighting the tools and learning them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. But I'd rather be the person who knows where the machine goes wrong than the person who refuses and can't pay rent. I'd learn the tools and still campaign against using them unchecked.

say: Drug companies save millions and **translators pay** for it.
A qualified human should **sign off** every patient document.
think: My agency could **halve its translators**, and I'm average, not top.
Checking work keeps coming, but at a **rate too low** to live on.
do: Help start a **translators' co-op** selling directly to hospitals and charities.
Take a **course** in the tools that have proven themselves.
Ask Noor about a **cheaper flat** next year.
feel: **Angry and frightened**, with some guilt about using the same tools.
S1.quote: I'd rather be the person who knows where the machine goes wrong than the person who refuses and can't pay rent.
fieldNote: She expects real **income loss** and sees herself below the cut line.
Her answer mixes **collective action** with learning tools once proven.
She names the **contradiction** herself and accepts it.

steps.text: Help start a translators' co-op selling to hospitals and charities
Take a course on checking machine-translated medical documents
Move with Noor to a cheaper flat next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a public response right now: income support, free retraining, and rules on who's responsible when the AI gets a medical translation wrong. I'd go on the marches. I'd also say to the clinic volunteers that people still need someone to sit with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think translation as a paid job is over for someone like me by 2028. The AI does the thinking part, and that's all of my job except the clinic. The robots coming three years later means nothing to me unless I switch to something physical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get into hospital work quickly, maybe as a patient liaison or a healthcare assistant, where my Spanish still helps and the job is partly hands-on. That gives me a few years before robots get there. I'd claim any support going and I'd move back in with my mum if I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, properly. Two years isn't long enough to train for anything, and I've got no money to train with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would moving back in with your mum mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum lives two hours away in a small town with no hospital jobs. So it would mean giving up the clinic and my friends. I'd do it, but only if the rent became impossible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the people at the clinic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the families at the clinic the truth. An app can read a housing form, but an app can't hold someone's hand when the answer is no. Then I'd go home and worry about my own rent.

say: We need **income support**, free retraining and rules on medical errors.
People at the clinic still need **someone beside them**.
think: Translation as a **paid job** is over for me by 2028.
The robot delay only helps if I **switch to physical** work.
do: Apply for **patient liaison** or healthcare assistant roles at the hospital.
Claim **any support** offered and march for more.
Move back to her **mum's house** if rent becomes impossible.
feel: **Properly scared**: two years and no money to train.
S2.quote: An app can read a housing form, but an app can't hold someone's hand when the answer is no.
fieldNote: She spots the **hands-on gap**: hospital work buys about three years.
Her fallback is **family**, at real cost to her life and the clinic.
Even in the fastest scenario she keeps the **clinic families** at the centre.

steps.text: Apply for patient liaison and healthcare assistant jobs at the hospital
Claim income support and join the marches for more
Move back to her mum's house if rent becomes impossible

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to get the rules right, so let's not waste the first three arguing. I'd push the co-op idea hard and I'd write to my representative about public funding for interpreter retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is just about enough to switch into healthcare without falling apart. I'd keep translating while the work lasts, probably two or three years, and use that money to train. But it's still the end of the career I trained for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start an evening healthcare assistant course and ask Dr Ruiz about bilingual research nurse roles. I'd translate as much as possible while rates hold, and put every spare bit aside. By year three I'd want to be working in the hospital, even part-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sad more than scared. There's a plan in this one, which I don't have in the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a research nurse rather than something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I already know trial paperwork backwards from translating it. A bilingual nurse who explains a consent form to a Spanish-speaking patient is the closest thing to my job that has a body in it. That stays useful for a few years after the AI arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut to save for training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Takeaways, mostly, and my gym. I'd walk to the hospital instead of the bus. It's not much, but at my level forty a month is a lot.

say: We have **five years** to get the rules right; let's not waste them.
think: Five years is just enough to **switch into healthcare**.
It's still the **end of the career** I trained for.
do: Start an **evening healthcare** assistant course in year one.
Ask Dr Ruiz about **bilingual research nurse** roles.
Translate while rates hold and **save** every spare bit.
feel: **Sad** more than scared, because there's a plan.
S3.quote: A bilingual nurse who explains a consent form to a Spanish-speaking patient is the closest thing to my job that has a body in it.
fieldNote: She still expects to **lose translation income**, but has time to land elsewhere.
Her switch builds on **trial paperwork** she already knows.

steps.text: Start an evening healthcare assistant course in the first year
Ask Dr Ruiz about bilingual research nurse openings
Drop takeaways and the gym to save forty a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this fairly, if we plan. I'd want the co-op running and the professional association negotiating with hospitals for human sign-off. Publicly I'd sound fairly calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd have six or seven more good years of translation, maybe with rates sliding. That's long enough to finish a nursing degree part-time. I'm 27, so at 37 I'd still be young for a new career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep translating and get the co-op going in the first year. In year two I'd apply for a part-time nursing degree and keep the clinic. I'd learn the AI tools properly once colleagues have worked out which ones are safe, because I'd need the speed to earn while studying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but OK. It's a long road, but I can see the end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does a decade change who you'd blame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. It's still companies deciding to cut people because it's cheaper. But with ten years there's no excuse for the government not to have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your mum say about you becoming a nurse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be thrilled, honestly. My mum never understood translating. She'd tell all her friends her daughter is a nurse, even before I'd started the course.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I've got no savings and no time to train. What would help is free retraining into healthcare and some income while I do it, so I'm not forced home to my mum's.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the patients. A consent form is a promise between a doctor and a scared person. If nobody checks the translation, nobody's checking the promise.

headlineQuote: A consent form is a promise between a doctor and a scared person. If nobody checks the translation, nobody's checking the promise.
portrait: Uma is a **27-year-old** Spanish–English medical translator who shares a flat and volunteers at a migrant clinic.
She relies on **one agency**, has a student loan and about three weeks saved.
She uses AI tools **only under pressure** and checks every line.
Progressive and practical, she pairs **campaigning** with learning proven tools.
Across scenarios she plans a move into **hospital care work**, which the extra time makes realistic.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she has no savings and no time to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: **Free retraining** into healthcare with some income while she studies.
